Iridium-Catalyzed Enantioselective Allenylic Cyanomethylation
Aditya Chakrabarty and Santanu Mukherjee*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2025, 27, 8752−8757

ABSTRACT: The poor acidity of acetonitrile restricted its utility as a
C2 synthon of a cyanomethyl group for incorporation into organic
compounds. We now employed a 2-azido allylic alcohol as an
acetonitrile enolate surrogate for the first enantioselective allenylic
cyanomethylation. This mild and base-free protocol utilizes cooperative
iridium and Lewis acid catalysis for the activation of branched allenylic
alcohols to deliver α-allenylic acetonitriles in moderate to good yields
with excellent enantioselectivity.
T
he ubiquitous occurrence of the cyanomethyl group
across a diverse array of bioactive molecules and natural
products (Figure 1) inspired the development of methods for
its introduction to organic compounds.
1
While acetonitrile
appears to be the most obvious choice, its use as the precursor
of cyanomethyl carbanion comes with serious synthetic hurdles
(Scheme 1A).
2
The attenuated acidity of the α-protons of acetonitrile
compared to carbonyls (pK
a
of CH
3
CN of ∼31.3 in DMSO)
3
makes it relatively difficult to deprotonate, and thus, it remains
inert toward electrophiles. In fact, the inertness of acetonitrile
is a reason for its choice as a solvent in many chemical
reactions. Although acetonitrile can be deprotonated using a
strong base, the “hardness” and ambiphilic nature of the
corresponding cyanomethyl anion makes its selective applica-
tion as a carbon nucleophile challenging.
4
Among other pathways, the base-mediated dimerization of
acetonitrile to β-enaminonitrile, called the Thorpe reaction
(Scheme 1A),
5
is known to compete with the direct addition of
the acetonitrile carbanion to a chosen electrophile. An
attempted Pd-catalyzed allylic alkylation of acetonitrile by

Ding, Hou, and co-workers resulted in α-allylation of β-
enaminonitrile through the intervention of the Thorpe
reaction.
6
While α-cyanoacetates have been utilized as masked
cyanomethyl precursors due to the enhanced acidity of its α-
proton, it adds an extra step to remove the carboxylate group
in the overall cyanomethylation sequence (Scheme 1B).
7
Despite other notable advancements (e.g., silyl ketene imines
as a cyanomethyl carbanion equivalent), only a handful of
enantioselective transformations have been reported.
8
Shibasaki and co-workers developed a general strategy for
activating alkyl nitriles through a cooperative combination of
Lewis acid with Brønsted base catalysis and accomplished
enantioselective addition to a series of electrophiles.
9
In a
recent study, Li et al. demonstrated a synergistic Rh and silane
catalysis strategy to tame the reactivity of the cyanomethyl
anion for enantioselective allylic substitution.
10
Taking a completely different approach to overcome the
challenges associated with the direct use of a cyanomethyl
carbanion, Cui et al. in 2017 introduced 2-azido allylic alcohol
1 as an acetonitrile enolate surrogate (Scheme 1B).
11
This
stable and easily accessible vinyl azide promises wide
applicability due to its apparent compatibility with a variety
of catalytic conditions for reactions proceeding under ionic or
radical pathways (Scheme 2A, eqs 1 and 2).
11,12
To date, the
only application of 1 in an enantioselective transformation is
reported by Cao et al. in Ir-catalyzed allylic substitution
(Scheme 2A, eq 3).
13
With our interest in vinyl azides
14
as a surrogate of amide or
ketone enolates, we applied them as a nucleophile in Ir-
catalyzed enantioselective allylic
15
and allenylic substitution
reactions.
16
As a part of this research program, we wondered
whether a similar catalytic concept could be extended to 2-
azido allylic alcohol (1) for achieving enantioselective allenylic
cyanomethylation. To the best of our knowledge, no α-
allenylation of alkyl nitriles (allenylic cyanoalkylation) has ever
been reported, let alone an enantioselective variant. Herein, we
present the first catalytic enantioselective allenylic cyanome-
thylation.
17
Although the Ir-catalyzed allenylic substitution reaction was
first introduced by the Takeuchi group in 2004,
18
its
enantioselective variant was not known until the seminal
development by Carreira et al. through the application of their
Ir(I)/(phosphoramidite,olefin) complex.
19
We envisioned the
interception of η
2
-Ir(I)-bound allenylic carbocation intermedi-
ate A, proposed to be generated from a branched allenylic
electrophile under cooperative Ir(I) and Lewis acid catal-
ysis,
19,20
with 2-azido allylic alcohol 1 (Scheme 2B). The
resulting α-allenylic iminodiazonium intermediate B was
expected to spontaneously extrude nitrogen and acetone to
generate α-allenylic acetonitrile.
To validate our catalytic hypothesis, we began our
investigation with the model reaction between 2-azido allylic
alcohol 1 and 1-phenyl allenyl alcohol 2a (Table 1). When the
reaction was carried out in THF at 50 °C using 6 mol % of an
in situ generated Ir complex derived from [Ir(COD)Cl]
2
and
Carreira’s (P,olefin) ligand (S
a
)-L1,
21
in the presence of 10
mol % Sc(OTf)
3
as the Lewis acidic promoter and 4 Å MS, the
desired α-allenylic acetonitrile 3a was formed in 34% yield
along with the homocoupled product 3a′ as a 1:1 inseparable
mixture (entry 1). Despite the low yield, the high enantiomeric
ratio (er) of 3a in this reaction was encouraging and called for
further optimization. We have recently disclosed the
homocoupling reaction of allenylic alcohols under divergent
cooperative catalysis and shown it to proceed through the
intermediacy of a cross-dienol intermediate generated via a 1,3-
hydroxy transposition of allenylic alcohol.
22
We wondered
whether the generation of cross-dienol could be avoided by
replacing allenylic alcohol with allenylic carbonate 2a′. A
reaction with 1.5 equiv of 2a′ under similar conditions afforded
a slightly improved ratio of 3a over 3a′ (entry 2). A careful
investigation revealed the formation of stable 4-phenyl 1,3-
butadien-2-ol-carbonate (3a″) via [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrange-
ment of 2a′ in this reaction. Although the use of 2.5 equiv of
2a′ improved the yield of 3a to 45%, a considerable amount of
the homocoupled product was observed (entry 3). When the
reaction was carried out at an ambient temperature in the
presence of 2 equiv of allenylic alcohol 2a, α-allenylic
acetonitrile 3a was isolated in 53% yield with 99:1 er and an
improved 3a to 3a′ ratio (5.5:1) (entry 4). Changing the
desiccant to 5 Å MS further enhanced the 3a/3a′ ratio, even
though it was at the cost of the yield (entry 5). Considering the
low nucleophilicity of 2-azido allylic alcohol 1 compared to the
in situ generated cross-dienol, we anticipated that maintaining a
low concentration of allenylic alcohols could be beneficial.
Accordingly, when 2a was employed as the limiting substrate,
the desired α-allenylic acetonitrile 3a was obtained almost
exclusively (23:1 3a/3a′) and isolated in 61% yield with
99.8:0.2 er (entry 6). (R

exclusively in 65% yield with excellent er (entry 9).
Efforts toward enhancing the yield of 3a further by varying
Lewis acidic promoters were ineffective (entries 10−12).
Increasing promoter loading to 20 mol % resulted in a poorer
3a/3a′ ratio (entry 13). The efficacy of the reaction remained
unaltered when the reaction was carried out on a 0.4 mmol
scale (entry 9 vs entry 14).
Having optimized the reaction conditions, we set out to
showcase the generality of this enantioselective allenylation of
2-azido allylic alcohol 1. As shown in Table 2, allenylic alcohols
bearing electron-rich as well as electron-deficient 1-aryl
substituents were well-accommodated, and the corresponding
α-allenylic acetonitriles (3a−3p) were obtained in moderate to
good yields and generally with excellent enantioselectivity.
Consistent with the proposed involvement of the allenylic
carbocation (A in Scheme 2B) in this reaction,
19
allenylic
alcohols containing an electron-rich aryl group generally
resulted in products with higher yields compared to those
bearing electron-deficient aryl substituents. Para- or meta-
substituted aryl rings on allenylic alcohol were found to be
better suited in this reaction compared to the ortho-substituted
ones. In the latter case, the products were obtained in lower
yields, although excellent enantioselectivity was maintained. A
low yield of 3m is in agreement with the lesser stability of the
corresponding allenylic carbocationic intermediate as well as
slow nucleophilic attack of 1, leading to faster decomposition
of allenylic alcohol 2m. Allenylic alcohols containing a
disubstituted electron-rich aryl group (2k and 2l) afforded
the products (3k and 3l) in moderate to good yields with high
er. Allenylic alcohols 2n−2p with polyaromatic substituents
delivered the products (3n−3p) in moderate yield while
maintaining outstanding enantioselectivities.
Allenylic alcohols substituted with heterocycles, such as 1,3-
benzodioxolane (2q) and differently substituted thienyls (2r
and 2s), are compatible with our reaction conditions.
However, the corresponding products (3q−3s) were obtained
in relatively low yields. Ferrocene-substituted allenylic alcohol
2t provided the α-allenylic acetonitrile in only 39% yield with
90:10 er. The lower enantioselectivity points toward the
competing background reaction, likely due to the ease of
formation and higher stability of the ferrocene-substituted free
allenylic carbocation.
23
Aliphatic allenylic alcohols failed to
participate in this allenylic cyanomethylation reaction,
presumably due to the lower stability of the corresponding
allenylic carbocation, which is a limitation of this catalyst
system. It is noted that the formation of no other side products
could be detected in any of these cases. The low yield of the
product in certain cases (3o−3q) can be attributed to the
decomposition of allenylic alcohol under Lewis acidic
conditions.
To showcase the scalability of our protocol, a reaction
between 2-azido allylic alcohol 1 and allenylic alcohol 2d was
carried out on a 1.0 mmol scale under our optimized reaction
conditions (Scheme 3A). The desired product 3d was isolated
in 55% yield with 99.5:0.5 er. The synthetic utility of α-
allenylic acetonitriles was illustrated through several synthetic
transformations involving 3d (Scheme 3B). Selective reduction
of the cyano group in 3d with DIBAL-H at 0 °C afforded α-
allenylic acetaldehyde 4 in 85% yield. This two-step process
represents the first formal α-allenylation of acetaldehyde. The
addition of the phenyl Grignard reagent to 4 followed by
oxidation of the resulting unpurified secondary alcohol (with
1:1 dr) led to the formation of α-allenylic acetophenone 5 in
91% yield over two steps with 99.5:0.5 er. The absolute
configuration of 5 was ascertained to be R by comparing its
specific rotation to that of a sample obtained through α-
allenylation of vinyl azide as a ketone enolate surrogate.
16
The
absolute configuration of other α-allenylic acetonitriles shown
in Table 2 was tentatively assigned as the same by analogy.
Reductive ozonolysis of 3d resulted in primary alcohol 6,
which was protected as carbamate 8. Reduction of 3d with
LiAlH
4
and Boc protection afforded N-Boc bis-homoallenylic
amine 9, which was subjected to Ag-catalyzed cyclization: 2,3-
disubtituted pyrrolidine 10 was obtained as a single
diastereomer in 43% yield over three steps with excellent
enantioselectivity.
24
No erosion of the enantiopurity was
observed in any of these reaction sequences. The Ritter
reaction of 3d with 1-adamantanol (11) furnished N-
adamantyl α-allenylic amide 12 in 67% yield.

due to the highly acidic conditions required for this reaction.
Nonetheless, this two-step functionalization provides an
alternative approach for the enantioselective synthesis of N-
alkyl-substituted α-allenylic amides.
In summary, we have developed the first catalytic
enantioselective allenylic cyanomethylation using 2-azido
allylic alcohol as acetonitrile enolate surrogate.
17
This
transformation proceeds through the cooperative activation
of branched allenylic alcohol by an Ir(I)/(P,olefin) complex
and Lewis acidic Sc(OTf)
3
and delivers α-allenylic acetonitriles
in moderate to good yields with outstanding enantioselectivity.
Easy accessibility of the substrates, base-free reaction
conditions, and ambient temperature are some of the practical
advantages of our protocol. Efforts toward the utilization of
this acetonitrile enolate surrogate in other catalytic enantiose-
lective transformations are currently underway in our
laboratory.

ABSTRACT: The poor acidity of acetonitrile restricted its utility as a
C2 synthon of a cyanomethyl group for incorporation into organic
compounds. We now employed a 2-azido allylic alcohol as an
acetonitrile enolate surrogate for the first enantioselective allenylic
cyanomethylation. This mild and base-free protocol utilizes cooperative
iridium and Lewis acid catalysis for the activation of branched allenylic
alcohols to deliver α-allenylic acetonitriles in moderate to good yields
with excellent enantioselectivity.

The attenuated acidity of the α-protons of acetonitrile

makes it relatively dificult to deprotonate, and thus, it remains
inert toward electrophiles. In fact, the inertness of acetonitrile
is a reason for its choice as a solvent in many chemical
reactions. Although acetonitrile can be deprotonated using a
strong base, the “hardness” and ambiphilic nature of the
corresponding cyanomethyl anion makes its selective applica-
tion as a carbon nucleophile challenging.<sup>4</sup>

Despite other notable advancements (e.g., silyl ketene imines
as a cyanomethyl carbanion equivalent), only a handful of
enantioselective transformations have been reported.<sup>8</sup>

Shibasaki and co-workers developed a general strategy for
activating alkyl nitriles through a cooperative combination of
Lewis acid with Brønsted base catalysis and accomplished
enantioselective addition to a series of electrophiles.<sup>9</sup> In a
recent study, Li et al. demonstrated a synergistic Rh and silane
catalysis strategy to tame the reactivity of the cyanomethyl
anion for enantioselective allylic substitution.<sup>10</sup>

Taking a completely diferent approach to overcome the
challenges associated with the direct use of a cyanomethyl
carbanion, Cui et al. in 2017 introduced 2-azido allylic alcohol
1 as an acetonitrile enolate surrogate (Scheme 1B).<sup>11</sup> This
stable and easily accessible vinyl azide promises wide
applicability due to its apparent compatibility with a variety
of catalytic conditions for reactions proceeding under ionic or
radical pathways (Scheme 2A, eqs 1 and 2).<sup>11,12</sup> To date, the
only application of 1 in an enantioselective transformation is
reported by Cao et al. in Ir-catalyzed allylic substitution
(Scheme 2A, eq 3).<sup>13</sup>

ketone enolates, we applied them as a nucleophile in Ir-

Having optimized the reaction conditions, we set out to
showcase the generality of this enantioselective allenylation of
2-azido allylic alcohol 1. As shown in Table 2, allenylic alcohols
bearing electron-rich as well as electron-deficient 1-aryl
substituents were well-accommodated, and the corresponding
α-allenylic acetonitriles (3a−3p) were obtained in moderate to
good yields and generally with excellent enantioselectivity.
Consistent with the proposed involvement of the allenylic
carbocation (A in Scheme 2B) in this reaction,<sup>19</sup>
allenylic

alcohols containing an electron-rich aryl group generally
resulted in products with higher yields compared to those
bearing electron-deficient aryl substituents. Para- or meta
substituted aryl rings on allenylic alcohol were found to be
better suited in this reaction compared to the ortho-substituted
ones. In the latter case, the products were obtained in lower
yields, although excellent enantioselectivity was maintained. A
low yield of 3m is in agreement with the lesser stability of the
corresponding allenylic carbocationic intermediate as well as
slow nucleophilic attack of 1, leading to faster decomposition
of allenylic alcohol 2m. Allenylic alcohols containing a
disubstituted electron-rich aryl group (2k and 2l) aforded

delivered the products (3n−3p) in moderate yield while
maintaining outstanding enantioselectivities.
